title: State Minimisation, Programmable Logic and Circuits
toolchain: no code on screen. Check every state table, row-matching step, implication-table entry and pass, equivalence claim (by partition refinement and by running input sequences from both states), product-term and lookup-table content, and every electronics number by exhaustive enumeration in Python 3.11.9, standard library only (itertools.product over states and input sequences): `python3 -I check.py`. The planner's results are in PLAN.md (Decisions, 'Checked'). No HDL or circuit simulator is installed (iverilog, yosys, ghdl, verilator, ngspice: none).

sources.note: Slides for the whole course (190 pp., two slides per page). This lecture is all of 'Sequential Logic: Further Considerations', pp. 144-162 (redundant states and row matching pp. 144-147; state equivalence and the implication table pp. 148-155; GLA and GAL pp. 156-158; FPGA and the Xilinx Spartan CLB pp. 158-162), then 'Electronics, Devices and Circuits: Underlying Concepts' up to Kirchhoff's voltage law, pp. 163-170. p. 170's last bullet (potential divider) and pp. 171+ are Lecture 12's. Refreshers from lectures outside our series: Mealy machines pp. 122-123 (Lecture 9); multiplexer as a 'hardware look-up table' p. 66, ROM p. 70-71, PLA and PAL pp. 71-73, SRAM volatile p. 73. pdftotext drops primes and some symbols, and loses the figures: read the tables and figures from the rendered page (pdftoppm), especially pp. 152-155 (implication tables), 157-160 (GLA, GAL, FPGA, CLB) and 170 (KVL loop). Slide slips: p. 160's CLB figure labels the F-LUT's output 'G' (should be F; the lecturer says so); p. 151-153 write '≠' for 'not equivalent' (we use ≢)
